newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU accuses six countries of breaking water laws.
newsitem.headline: EU accuses six countries of breaking water laws.

text.p: Belgium and Ireland have broken EU rules intended to stop water being polluted with dangerous substances, the European Commission said on Friday.
It said it was taking Belgium to court and had sent Ireland a final warning which could be followed by court action.
"The Commission has decided to take further steps in legal action against Belgium and Ireland for failing to respect (EU laws) on dangerous substances in water," the statement said.
In a separate statement, the Commission also launched water-related cases against Spain, Greece, Italy and France.

"The case against Belgium relates to a failure to adopt and communicate (to the Commission) pollution reduction programmes for a number of substances singled out for priority action... because of their toxicity, persistence or tendency to bio-accumulate," the first statement said.
Bio-accumulation is the process by which toxins build up in the bodies of living organisms, damaging their health.
"The case against Ireland relates principally to a failure to establish binding water quality objectives, particularly for the substance phosphorous.

"An increase in discharges of this substance over the past two decades, especially from agricultural sources, has led to a decline in water quality, particularly in several important Irish lakes, such as Lough Derg and Lough Conn," it said.

It said it was also taking Spain, Italy and Greece to court and had sent France a warning letter for what it said was their failure to follow EU rules intended to tackle pollution from high nitrate concentrations in farm water run-off.
